Subject: Performance deep dive: streaming & token limits for Acme SDK

Hi Lauren / Ben,

Thanks again for the call earlier — super helpful. Attached is a small production-like traffic sample (anonymized) and a short summary of our expected usage patterns. A few clarifications from our side to help scope the PoC: 

- Latency SLO: p95 end-to-end for user-facing chat should be <= 150ms when under normal load.
- Peak throughput: we expect bursts to ~220 requests/s for short periods (1-2 minutes) with sustained baseline ~40 req/s.
- Concurrency: typical concurrent sessions of 30-60, average 45.
- Streaming: client requires token-level streaming over a persistent WS for realtime UX; partial tokens acceptable as they arrive.
- Context: many sessions will include a medium history + 6k tokens of user docs (input) and expected output up to 3k tokens on long summaries.

Key asks: can you outline the PoC plan, initial configuration you’d run (model variants, batching, autoscale settings), and what metrics/telemetry we should instrument? Also list any tradeoffs (quantization, batching vs streaming latency) we should expect.

Cheers,
Alice
Alice Smith
Head of Platform Integrations
Acme Corporation

Subject: Re: Performance deep dive: streaming & token limits for Acme PoC

Alice — thanks for the sample and the clear SLOs. Below is a concise PoC plan and the tradeoffs to expect. I’ve highlighted immediate asks from your side.

Post-call PoC plan (high level) — 3 weeks
1) Week 0: alignment & test data
  - Redwood: spin up a dedicated PoC sandbox (VPC-isolated) with observability hooks.
  - Acme: provide 2 representative traffic slices (realtime chat + long-summary).
2) Week 1: baseline runs (no quantization)
  - Run steady-state at baseline 40 req/s and short burst tests to 220 req/s.
  - Validate p95 < 150ms for simple prompts; capture token-level latencies.
3) Week 2: streaming & concurrency tests
  - Enable streaming via persistent WS; measure first-byte latency, p50/p95/p99 for partial-chunk delivery.
  - Increase concurrent sessions to 60 and test autoscaling triggers.
4) Week 3: optimize and report
  - Try model variants (higher capacity vs quantized) and recommend final config.
  - Deliver runbook + rollback plan + estimated monthly cost.

Initial config proposal (starter)
- Model variant: rdx-3.7-8k (full-precision) for baseline; rdx-3.7-8k-q4 for cost/throughput trade tests.
- Serving: dedicated pool with KV cache warmed for common prefixes; continuous batching window 5-10ms for safety.
- Autoscale: target CPU/GPU occupancy trigger at 65% with burst buffer for 30s to absorb spikes.
- Networking: websocket endpoint for streaming; enable keepalive and per-connection rate limits.

Tradeoffs & expectations
- Streaming vs batching: aggressive batching reduces cost but increases first-byte latency. For your 150ms p95 target we recommend conservative batching (5-10ms) and prioritize low-latency routing.
- Quantization: q4 significantly reduces GPU memory and increases throughput but can add ~10-25ms in decoding latency depending on model and token size — test with your long-summary prompts.
- Context size: 9k total (6k input + up to 3k output) increases per-token compute; expect p95 to grow nonlinearly as output approaches 3k. Consider early-stopping/summary heuristics for very long outputs.

Instrumentation & success metrics
- Per-token latency traces (first-byte, per-chunk, final token).
- Inference-level metrics: tokens/s, GPU utilization, batching window distribution, KV cache hit rate.
- Business metrics: percent of sessions meeting p95 < 150ms, cost per 1k tokens.

Immediate asks from Acme
- Confirm dataset slices to use for the PoC by Wed 2026-07-01.
- Confirm which latency threshold is mandatory vs aspirational (150ms p95 is mandatory?).
- Any network constraints (e.g., SES/edge locations) we should provision for?

Next steps
- If that plan looks good I’ll provision the sandbox and loop in Ben for infra runbooks. Propose 30-minute kick-off on Fri 2026-07-02.

Thanks,
Lauren Bishop

Subject: Re: Performance deep dive: streaming & token limits for Acme PoC — engineering notes

Quick engineering runbook and observations based on Acme's sample (I pulled a small slice):

Key observations from sample
- Average prompt length ~2.6k tokens, but ~8% of sessions push >6k input tokens with long histories.
- Output distribution: median ~400 tokens, tail up to 2.8k when doing full-document summaries.

Engineering suggestions
1) Model / quantization
  - Start with rdx-3.7-8k baseline (fp16) for initial latency targets. For cost testing use rdx-3.7-8k-q4; expect throughput +40% but +15-30ms decode overhead in our infra for long sequences.
2) Batching / streaming hybrid
  - Implement a hybrid path: streaming clients get a low-latency path (batch window <=5ms) with smaller micro-batches; non-streaming or bulk jobs use aggressive batching (20-50ms).
  - Use dynamic batching that falls back to streaming path if request has streaming flag.
3) KV cache & prefix caching
  - Warm KV cache for common system prompts and long user docs; a warm cache reduces token compute by avoiding re-encoding repeated context.
4) Autoscale & burst handling
  - Configure warm slots that can be provisioned in ~30s to handle 220 req/s bursts. Add a short-term buffer in queue to avoid outright failures on spikes.

Canary & telemetry plan
- Canary targets: run a 2-hour canary at 40 req/s, then stress 5-minute bursts at 220 req/s, and long-run at 60 concurrent sessions.
- Track: p50/p95/p99 user-perceived latency, first-byte time for streaming, tokens/sec, GPU occupancy, batch sizes, and qps by model variant.

Risks / mitigation
- Long outputs increase end-to-end latency nonlinearly — mitigate with streaming partial outputs and early stopping thresholds.
- Quantized models might introduce slight quality drift for long summaries; include a small human-eval sample in Week 2.

I’ll attach a small runbook snapshot and a sample infra config. Ben
